lesson.title: Fractions and Decimals: Same Number, Two Outfits
lesson.summary: Fractions and decimals are two different notations for the same underlying value, and the ACT rewards students who can move fluently between them and combine fractions with unlike denominators without hesitation.
lesson.body:
A fraction like 3/4 is not a mysterious symbol, it is a division problem waiting to happen: 3 divided by 4. That single idea explains why every fraction has an equivalent decimal form, and why decimals and fractions can always be converted into each other. Understanding this connection early matters because ACT problems rarely announce which form you should use. Sometimes a fraction is easier to work with, sometimes a decimal is, and the fastest test takers switch between them without a second thought.

Adding or subtracting fractions requires a common denominator, and the reason is more than a rule to memorize. You cannot add 3 fourths and 5 sixths directly for the same reason you cannot add 3 apples and 5 oranges and call the result 8 of anything useful: the pieces are different sizes. A fourth of something and a sixth of something are not the same size piece, so before you can combine them you have to rewrite both fractions using pieces of the same size, a common denominator. For 3/4 + 5/6, the smallest shared denominator is 12, since both 4 and 6 divide evenly into it. Rewriting: 3/4 becomes 9/12, and 5/6 becomes 10/12. Now the pieces match, and you can add the numerators directly: 9/12 + 10/12 = 19/12, which simplifies to the mixed number 1 and 7/12. You can check this by estimating in decimals: 3/4 is 0.75 and 5/6 is about 0.8333, and 0.75 + 0.8333 is about 1.5833, which matches 19/12 exactly.

Converting a fraction to a decimal is just carrying out the division the fraction represents. Take 5/8: dividing 5 by 8 gives 0.625. You can verify this the same way you would check any division, by multiplying back: 0.625 times 8 equals 5. Some fractions convert to decimals that terminate cleanly, like 5/8, while others repeat forever, like 1/3, which becomes 0.333 with the 3 continuing endlessly. Recognizing which fractions terminate (those whose denominator, once simplified, only has 2s and 5s as prime factors) can save time on the ACT when you are deciding whether to round or work with an exact fraction.

Multiplying fractions is more forgiving than adding them: there is no need for a common denominator, you simply multiply the numerators together and the denominators together. Dividing fractions uses the same multiplication rule after one extra step, flipping the second fraction upside down, because dividing by a number is the same as multiplying by its reciprocal. These two operations, along with the addition and conversion skills above, form the toolkit you will lean on constantly once ratios, proportions, and later algebraic equations start asking you to simplify messier expressions.
